interactions.label: Why must every consent discussion for pelvic gynaecological surgery specifically

params.question: Why must every consent discussion for pelvic gynaecological surgery specifically address the risk of ureteric injury?

answers.text: Because the ureter lies close to three surgical danger points — the ovarian vessels, the uterine artery, and the lateral vaginal wall

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The ureter crosses three danger points during pelvic surgery: near the infundibulopelvic ligament (ovarian vessels), beneath the uterine artery ('water under the bridge'), and beside the lateral vaginal wall. Injury at any of these points can cause obstruction or fistula formation.

answers.text: Because the ureter is the most commonly transected structure during Caesarean section

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While ureteric injury can occur during Caesarean section, the reason it is a consent essential for all pelvic surgery is its proximity to three specific surgical danger points throughout the pelvis — the ovarian vessels, the uterine artery, and the vaginal sidewall.

answers.text: Because ureteric injury is always irreversible and leads to nephrectomy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ureteric injury is not always irreversible — many injuries can be repaired with re-implantation or stenting. The reason it is highlighted in consent is that the ureter passes close to three danger points in the pelvis, making it vulnerable during routine pelvic surgical steps.

answers.text: Because the ureter cannot be visualised by any imaging modality preoperatively

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The ureter can be visualised preoperatively by CT urography, MRI, or intravenous urography. The consent requirement exists because the ureter runs close to three surgical danger points — near the ovarian vessels, under the uterine artery, and beside the vaginal sidewall — placing it at risk during dissection.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the three danger points: the ureter passes near the ovarian vessels (infundibulopelvic ligament), beneath the uterine artery, and beside the lateral vaginal wall. This is why ureteric injury is a standard consent topic for all pelvic surgery.
Well done. Understanding the ureter's three danger points is fundamental to safe pelvic surgery and informed consent.

interactions.label: During a combined D&C with endocervical curettage, the endocervical sample shoul

params.question: During a combined D&C with endocervical curettage, the endocervical sample should be collected after cervical dilatation to ensure a wider canal and a more representative specimen.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. Although a wider canal might seem to yield a better sample, dilating the cervix first allows endometrial cells to wash into the cervical canal and contaminate the endocervical specimen. ECC must always be performed before dilatation to preserve its diagnostic accuracy.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. Endocervical curettage must be performed before cervical dilatation. Dilating the canal first allows endometrial tissue to contaminate the endocervical sample, destroying its diagnostic value for detecting endocervical pathology.

interactions.label: A 35-year-old woman with second-degree uterovaginal prolapse and cervical elonga

params.question: A 35-year-old woman with second-degree uterovaginal prolapse and cervical elongation wishes to preserve her fertility. Fothergill's operation is planned. What is the most important point to include in her preoperative counselling?

answers.text: She will be unable to conceive naturally after the procedure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Fothergill's operation preserves the uterus by amputating the elongated cervix and repositioning the cardinal ligaments. Conception remains possible, but the mode of delivery is what changes — future pregnancies require Caesarean section.

answers.text: Any future pregnancy will require delivery by Caesarean section

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Fothergill's (Manchester) operation amputates the elongated cervix and repositions the cardinal ligaments while preserving the uterus. Because the cervix is shortened and the supporting structures are altered, vaginal delivery is no longer safe, and any future pregnancy must be delivered by Caesarean section.

answers.text: The prolapse will inevitably recur within five years and require repeat surgery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While prolapse recurrence is possible, it is not inevitable. The key counselling point for a woman wanting future pregnancies is that Fothergill's operation mandates Caesarean delivery, because the cervix is amputated and the cardinal ligaments are repositioned.

answers.text: Anterior and posterior colporrhaphy must be performed simultaneously to prevent recurrence

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Colporrhaphy may or may not be needed depending on the degree of cystocoele or rectocoele present. The most important counselling point for a woman of reproductive age undergoing Fothergill's operation is that future pregnancies will require Caesarean delivery.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key point is that Fothergill's operation preserves the uterus but amputates the cervix, so any future pregnancy must be delivered by Caesarean section. This is the critical fertility trade-off that must be discussed preoperatively.
Well done. The mandatory Caesarean delivery requirement is the most important fertility trade-off to discuss when Fothergill's operation is planned for a woman who wishes to bear children.

interactions.label: During a D&C for abnormal uterine bleeding, the uterine sound suddenly advances

params.question: During a D&C for abnormal uterine bleeding, the uterine sound suddenly advances 3 cm beyond the previously measured cavity depth with a clear loss of resistance. There is no active bleeding. What is the most appropriate next step?

answers.text: Complete the curettage carefully and discharge the patient the same day

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Continuing curettage after suspected perforation risks enlarging the defect and causing bowel or vascular injury. The sudden loss of resistance with excessive depth strongly suggests fundal perforation, which requires inpatient observation even without active bleeding.

answers.text: Observe the patient for 24 to 48 hours for signs of intraperitoneal bleeding or bowel injury

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. When perforation occurs with a small instrument (sound) and there is no active bleeding or suspicion of bowel injury, conservative management with inpatient observation for 24–48 hours is appropriate. Vital signs, abdominal examination, and haemoglobin monitoring guide further management.

Laparotomy is reserved for cases with active intraperitoneal bleeding, confirmed bowel injury, or perforation during evacuation of retained products. A sound perforation without bleeding is managed conservatively with observation — unnecessary laparotomy adds surgical morbidity.

answers.text: Insert intrauterine balloon tamponade and discharge after 6 hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Balloon tamponade is used for uterine haemorrhage, not for managing a suspected perforation. With a sound perforation and no active bleeding, the correct approach is inpatient observation for 24–48 hours to watch for delayed bleeding or peritoneal signs.

overallFeedback.feedback: A sudden loss of resistance with the instrument advancing beyond measured cavity depth indicates uterine perforation — typically at the thin fundus. Without active bleeding or suspected bowel injury, conservative observation for 24–48 hours is the standard management.
Well done. You correctly identified that a sound perforation without bleeding warrants conservative observation, reserving surgical intervention for more severe presentations.

interactions.label: A 26-year-old woman undergoes D&C for retained products of conception at 8 weeks

params.question: A 26-year-old woman undergoes D&C for retained products of conception at 8 weeks postpartum. Six months later, she presents with secondary amenorrhoea and inability to conceive. What is the most likely diagnosis?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cervical stenosis can cause haematometra and dysmenorrhoea but is less likely to cause complete amenorrhoea with infertility in this context. Postpartum D&C carries up to 30% risk of Asherman syndrome, making intrauterine adhesions the more likely diagnosis.

Sheehan syndrome follows massive postpartum haemorrhage causing pituitary ischaemia. This scenario describes a straightforward postpartum D&C without haemorrhage. The combination of amenorrhoea and infertility after postpartum curettage points strongly to Asherman syndrome.

Correct. Postpartum D&C carries the highest risk of Asherman syndrome — up to 30% in some series. The soft, adherent postpartum endometrium is vulnerable to basalis layer stripping during curettage, leading to intrauterine adhesions that cause amenorrhoea and infertility.

Endometritis is an early complication (within two weeks), presenting with fever and pelvic pain. The six-month interval, amenorrhoea, and infertility pattern after postpartum curettage strongly suggest Asherman syndrome — the most clinically significant late complication of D&C.

overallFeedback.feedback: Postpartum D&C has the highest risk of Asherman syndrome (intrauterine adhesions) — up to 30%. The soft postpartum endometrium is susceptible to basalis layer injury during curettage, leading to adhesions, amenorrhoea, and infertility. This is the key late complication to counsel about.
Well done. Recognising Asherman syndrome as the most likely diagnosis after postpartum D&C is essential for counselling patients about this specific risk before the procedure.
